21039:
The most thorough attack on the other gods came under King Josiah of Judah, around 622–621 BC, after a 'book of the law' was found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:8). Josiah burned the vessels made for Baal, Asherah and 'all the host of heaven' outside Jerusalem; removed the priests who burned incense to Baal, the sun, the moon and the constellations; took the Asherah out of the temple, burned it at the Kidron, ground it to powder and scattered the dust on common graves; broke down the houses of the cult prostitutes where women wove for Asherah; defiled Topheth so that no one could burn a child there; removed the horses dedicated to the sun and burned the chariots of the sun; and destroyed Solomon's shrines to Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (2 Kgs 23:4-14).

The reform did not last. Jeremiah and Ezekiel still condemn idolatry after Josiah's death (Jer 44; Ezek 8). But the Babylonian conquest in 586 BC changed everything. In the ancient view, a defeated nation's god had lost. The prophets argued the opposite: Yahweh had used Babylon to judge his people, and he was not tied to a land. Ezekiel saw God's glory by a canal in Babylon (Ezek 1:1-28), and Second Isaiah (Isa 40–48, written in the exile according to most scholars) declared that the gods of Babylon were nothing and that Yahweh alone controlled history (Isa 44:6-8; Isa 46:1-2).

After the exile, the worship of other gods largely disappears as a mainstream option within Judaism. The struggles of the Maccabean period were against Greek religion imposed from outside, not against Baal or Asherah. How far the exile created this change, and how far it confirmed an older faith, is part of the debate on monotheism in Israel.
21040: Scholars disagree about how much of 2 Kings 23 describes what Josiah actually did and how much reflects later idealising. Many think the core reform is historical; some think its scale has been enlarged. Archaeology (for example the buried Arad shrine) can be read either way.
21041: From gods to demons, and what it means today
21042:
Even before the exile, some texts say that the nations' gods were really 'devils' (shedim, demons): Israel 'sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not' (Deut 32:17; compare Ps 106:37 and the goat-demons of Lev 17:7). When Jewish scholars translated the Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they rendered 'all the gods of the nations are idols' in Ps 96:5 as 'all the gods of the nations are demons' (daimonia). Paul combines both ideas: an idol is nothing (1 Cor 8:4), yet what pagans sacrifice they offer 'to devils, and not to God' (1 Cor 10:20). Revelation speaks of people who 'worship devils, and idols of gold' (Rev 9:20).

Later tradition went further. Beelzebul became the prince of demons in the Gospels (Mark 3:22). Medieval and early modern magical books made Astaroth (Astarte, now male) a duke of hell, and John Milton's *Paradise Lost* (1667, book 1) gave a whole catalogue of fallen angels named after Old Testament gods: Moloch, Chemosh, Baalim and Ashtaroth, Thammuz, Dagon, Rimmon. These are literary and folk developments, not biblical teaching, but they show how the gods of Canaan lived on in the Christian imagination.

What does it mean today? Most Christians and Jews do not face statues of Baal. But the reasons Israel turned to other gods are familiar: security, prosperity, fertility, political advantage, family habit. The New Testament applies the idea of idolatry to greed (Col 3:5) and to anything that takes God's place (1 John 5:21); Jesus warns that no one can serve God and mammon (Matt 6:24). Paul's speech in Athens shows another side: he engages respectfully with people who worship 'an unknown god' and proclaims the Creator to them (Acts 17:22-31). The Bible's story ends with every nation's people, not their gods, worshipping before God's throne (Rev 7:9-10).
21043: The detailed hierarchies of demons named after ancient gods (Astaroth, Beelzebub, Moloch) come from medieval magical literature and from Milton, not from the Bible.

21148: What is the 'divine council' that some scholars find in the Bible? Which passages describe it, what does the Deuteronomy 32:8 variant change, and how strong are the objections and alternative readings?
21149: Several Bible passages picture God as a king holding court in heaven, surrounded by heavenly beings who stand before him, discuss, and carry out his decisions (1 Kgs 22:19-23; Job 1:6; Ps 82; Dan 7:9-10). Many scholars call this the 'divine council'. Some, especially Michael Heiser, build a whole-Bible story from it: God's council, rebellions by some of its members, the nations placed under lesser 'sons of God' after Babel (Deut 32:8, in its Qumran form), and Jesus reclaiming the nations from those powers. Others accept the council scenes but read key texts differently: the 'gods' of Psalm 82 as human judges, the 'sons of God' in Genesis 6 as Sethites or kings, 'Let us make man' as the Trinity or a plural of majesty, and the Hebrew 'sons of Israel' in Deut 32:8 as original. Critical historians see the council as a remnant of older Canaanite religion. All of these views agree that the Bible presents one God who alone is Creator and alone deserves worship.
21150: Heavenly court scenes are clearly in the Bible: Micaiah's vision, Job's prologue, Isaiah's call, Daniel's throne vision.
21151: 'Elohim' can refer to beings other than Israel's God, such as the dead Samuel and foreign gods; what that implies is debated.
21152: Deut 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' in the traditional Hebrew text but 'sons of God' in a Qumran scroll and the Greek tradition; many modern translations follow the latter.
21153: The 'three rebellions' (Eden, Genesis 6, Babel) and 'reclaiming the nations' are a synthesis by some scholars, not a reading all accept.
21154: Alternatives remain strong: human judges in Psalm 82, Sethite or royal readings of Genesis 6, Trinitarian or majestic readings of 'Let us'.
21155: No mainstream view treats council members as gods to be worshipped; the debate is about what kinds of beings exist and how the texts describe them.
21157:
Ancient people often pictured their chief god as a king with a court. At Ugarit, the high god El presides over 'the assembly of El' and 'the sons of El' on a mountain. Babylonian texts describe the gods meeting to decide destinies. The Bible uses similar pictures. God sits on a throne with 'all the host of heaven standing by him' (1 Kgs 22:19); the 'sons of God' come to present themselves before him (Job 1:6); he is 'greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints' (Ps 89:7); in Daniel's vision 'thousand thousands ministered unto him… the judgment was set, and the books were opened' (Dan 7:10).

The differences matter as much as the similarities. In the Bible, God does not need advice and is never outvoted. The council beings are his creatures (Neh 9:6; Ps 148:2-5) and his servants. They report, praise, volunteer and carry out tasks. Prophets claim to have 'stood in the counsel of the LORD' and so to speak his word (Jer 23:18; Jer 23:22).

The phrase 'divine council' is a scholarly label. Some scholars use it simply for these court scenes. Others, especially in recent evangelical teaching, make it a key to the whole Bible. This guide sets out the texts and the main ways they are read.
21159:
The Hebrew word elohim is plural in form but usually means 'God' when it refers to Israel's God, which it does about 2,500 times. Yet the same word is used of other beings. Foreign gods are elohim: Chemosh is the elohim of Moab (Judg 11:24). The medium at Endor sees the dead Samuel as 'elohim ascending out of the earth' (1 Sam 28:13). Psalm 82 says God judges 'among the elohim'. Psalm 8:5 says humans were made 'a little lower than elohim', which the Greek translation and Heb 2:7 render 'angels'. Some older translations take elohim in Exod 22:8-9 as 'judges'.

Divine-council scholars such as Michael Heiser conclude that elohim describes a kind of being whose proper home is the spiritual world, not a set of divine attributes. On this view, 'Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh': he alone is uncreated, all-powerful and worthy of worship. Others think this goes too far. They argue that the word's wide use is simply flexible language, as English 'god' can be used of a celebrity or a belly (Phil 3:19), and that biblical writers increasingly deny that other gods are real (Isa 44:9; Jer 10:10-11).

Both sides agree that the Bible never treats other elohim as equal to Yahweh. He is 'God of gods' (Deut 10:17), 'great King above all gods' (Ps 95:3), and the one before whom all gods bow (Ps 97:7).
21160: Heiser's description of elohim as a 'place of residence' term is his own proposal. Many scholars accept that the word covers various spiritual beings but do not adopt that definition.
21162:
The clearest council scene is Micaiah's vision before Ahab's last battle. Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven on both sides. God asks who will entice Ahab to his death; various beings make suggestions, and a spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths (1 Kgs 22:19-23). In Job's prologue the 'sons of God' present themselves, and among them comes 'the satan', literally 'the accuser', who questions Job's motives (Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-6). Hebrew has the definite article ('the accuser'), so many scholars think this is a title for a court official rather than a personal name; how this figure relates to the later Satan is debated.

Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned, surrounded by seraphim, and hears him ask, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' (Isa 6:1-8). Psalm 89 praises God in 'the congregation of the saints' (Ps 89:5-7). The king of Babylon boasts that he will sit on 'the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north' (Isa 14:13), echoing the language of a divine mountain. In Daniel's vision thrones are set, the court sits, and 'one like the Son of man' comes with the clouds to receive dominion over all nations (Dan 7:9-14). Jesus applies this to himself at his trial (Mark 14:62). In Revelation God's throne is surrounded by twenty-four elders on thrones and living creatures (Rev 4:2-11).

Psalm 82 is the most debated scene: God judges 'among the gods' and sentences them to die like men. Whether those 'gods' are heavenly beings, human judges or Israel at Sinai is discussed in its own debate.
21164:
Three times in Genesis God speaks in the plural: 'Let us make man in our image' (Gen 1:26); 'the man is become as one of us' (Gen 3:22); 'let us go down, and there confound their language' (Gen 11:7). Isaiah's 'who will go for us?' (Isa 6:8) is similar. Readers have explained this in four main ways.

The council reading says God is addressing his heavenly court, announcing a decision in which they share as witnesses, though God alone creates (Gen 1:27 returns to the singular: 'God created'). Many Jewish interpreters, including Rashi, read 1:26 this way, as do many modern scholars. The Trinitarian reading, common among the Church Fathers, sees a hint of the plurality within the one God, later revealed as Father, Son and Spirit (John 1:1-3; Col 1:16). The plural of majesty reading compares a king's royal 'we', though critics note that this usage is not clearly attested in biblical Hebrew. The plural of deliberation reading sees God speaking to himself, as a person says 'let's see'.

These options are not all exclusive. Some Christian interpreters hold that the original setting is a council address, while the fuller meaning in the light of the New Testament is Trinitarian.
21165: The council reading does not say angels created humans or share God's image-giving power. Its defenders stress that Gen 1:27 attributes creation to God alone.
21167:
The Song of Moses says that when the Most High divided the nations, 'he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance' (Deut 32:8-9). That is the reading of the traditional Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text), followed by the KJV, NASB and NIV.

But a Hebrew manuscript of Deuteronomy found at Qumran (4QDeut-j, from Cave 4, discovered in 1952) reads 'sons of God' (bene elohim). The Greek Septuagint reads 'angels of God' in most manuscripts and 'sons of God' in some. Many textual scholars think 'sons of God' is original and that a later scribe changed it to 'sons of Israel', perhaps because it seemed to suggest many gods. The harder reading is often the original one, and 'sons of Israel' makes poor sense, since Israel did not yet exist when the nations were divided (Gen 10–11). The RSV, NRSV, ESV and NET follow the Qumran and Greek reading in some form.

On the council reading, this verse explains a lot: after Babel God allotted the nations to lesser heavenly beings and kept Israel for himself. That is why Deuteronomy says God 'divided' the sun, moon and stars to the nations (Deut 4:19) and speaks of gods 'whom he had not given unto them' (Deut 29:26), and why Daniel mentions heavenly 'princes' of Persia and Greece (Dan 10:13; Dan 10:20). Others accept 'sons of God' but take them simply as angels who serve God among the nations, or argue that the Masoretic reading reflects a genuine tradition linking the nations to Israel's seventy members (Gen 46:27; Exod 1:5).
21168: Three rebellions? A synthesis and its critics
21169:
Some divine-council writers, Heiser especially, read Genesis 1–11 as three rebellions by heavenly beings that explain the state of the world. First, Eden: the serpent (nachash) is a council member who deceives humanity and is cursed (Gen 3:1-15); Christians identify him with Satan (Rev 12:9; Rev 20:2). Heiser's suggestion that nachash also plays on 'diviner' and 'shining one' is a word-play many scholars think is unlikely. Second, Genesis 6: the 'sons of God' cross into the human world and father the Nephilim (Gen 6:1-4), echoed in Jude 1:6 and 2 Pet 2:4. Third, Babel: humanity unites against God, and God scatters the nations and places them under the 'sons of God' (Gen 11:1-9; Deut 32:8), some of whom then rule badly and become the nations' gods (Ps 82).

This reading has real strengths: it connects passages that are often treated in isolation, and it explains why the New Testament speaks of 'principalities' and 'powers' (Eph 6:12; Col 2:15). But each link is debated. The serpent is not called a council member in Genesis. Genesis 6 has strong human readings (Sethites, royal tyrants). Babel does not mention the sons of God. And much of the detail comes from Second Temple books such as 1 Enoch, which, though old and influential, are not part of most Christian Bibles.

A fair summary is that the three-rebellion story is an interpretive synthesis. It is held by a growing number of evangelical teachers, but it is not the consensus of biblical scholars, and many careful readers prefer to keep the Bible's own statements and the synthesis distinct.
21171:
Whatever one makes of the council, the Bible clearly tells a story in which God, who chose Israel, intends to bring all nations back. Abraham is called so that 'all families of the earth' will be blessed (Gen 12:3). Psalm 82 ends, 'Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations' (Ps 82:8). Daniel's Son of Man receives a kingdom 'that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him' (Dan 7:14). The risen Jesus says all authority is his and sends his followers to 'all nations' (Matt 28:18-19).

Council readers add detail. Pentecost, where people from many nations hear God's works in their own languages (Acts 2:5-11), reverses Babel's confusion of languages. Some scholars, such as James M. Scott, argue that Luke's list of nations and Paul's plans echo the Table of Nations in Genesis 10; this is a debated hypothesis. Paul describes Christ disarming 'principalities and powers' (Col 2:15) and the church making God's wisdom known to them (Eph 3:10). He calls former gods those 'which by nature are no gods' (Gal 4:8) and plans to go as far as Spain (Rom 15:24; Rom 15:28), which some link to Tarshish, the far west of the known world (Isa 66:19), though the identification of Tarshish is itself uncertain.

The end of the story is a renewed council. In Revelation the Lamb is worthy because he redeemed people 'out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation' (Rev 5:9), the nations walk in the light of the city (Rev 21:24), and the leaves of the tree are 'for the healing of the nations' (Rev 22:2). Believers are called God's sons (Rom 8:14; Gal 3:26), will judge angels (1 Cor 6:3) and will reign with Christ (Rev 3:21; Rev 22:5).
21173:
Is this polytheism? Council defenders say no: the council beings are created (Col 1:16), subordinate and even mortal (Ps 82:7), and only Yahweh is worshipped. Classical monotheists reply that the Bible's strongest statements go beyond 'no rival': 'there is no God beside me' (Isa 45:5) and idols are 'nothing' (Isa 41:24). Council defenders answer that Babylon and Nineveh use the same 'none beside me' phrase of themselves (Isa 47:8; Zeph 2:15), so it means incomparability; many scholars, however, still read Second Isaiah as explicit monotheism. Paul holds both together: idols are nothing, yet demons are real (1 Cor 8:4-6; 1 Cor 10:19-21).

For particular texts, the alternatives are serious. Psalm 82's 'gods' have long been read as human judges (Calvin, Rashi) or as Israel at Sinai (rabbinic tradition), readings that fit Jesus' use in John 10 well. The 'sons of God' in Genesis 6 have been read as Sethites (Augustine, Calvin) or as kings (Targums, Kline). 'Let us' has Trinitarian and majestic readings. Deut 32:8 has a defensible traditional text. Critical historians such as Mark S. Smith accept that the council texts describe divine beings but see them as remnants of Israel's older, polytheistic religion, not as a consistent biblical theology.

There is also a practical objection. Popular teaching on territorial spirits, spiritual mapping or hidden giants can grow out of council language far beyond what the texts say. Responsible defenders of the council reading warn against this as strongly as their critics do.
21174: Myth: 'The divine council view says Christians should honour lesser gods.' Fact: no defender teaches that. The view is about what beings exist; worship belongs to God alone (Exod 20:3; Rev 22:8-9).
21175: What this means for reading the Bible
21176:
Whatever view you take, the council passages remind readers that the Bible's world is larger than the visible one. Prayer, worship and mission are pictured as happening before a heavenly court (Heb 12:22-24; Rev 5:8-14). The struggle against evil is described not only as human politics but as a struggle against spiritual powers (Eph 6:12), which is a reason for humility and prayer rather than fear or speculation.

The passages also keep returning to justice. Psalm 82's rulers are condemned for neglecting the poor and fatherless (Ps 82:3-4), whoever they are. The nations' gods fail because they cannot save (Isa 45:20). The Son of Man's kingdom is everlasting and just (Dan 7:14).

Finally, the council texts show that the Bible's confession of one God is not thin. God is not lonely or abstract; he is the King of a vast creation, surrounded by worshipping beings, who chooses to share his rule with redeemed humans (Rev 3:21). Christians read this, in the end, through Jesus, who has 'gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him' (1 Pet 3:22).
